opus-5.5.text:
I think the commitment goes deeper than any one executive. Leadership changes, but the strategic logic behind AI for Science at Google has been consistent for close to a decade, and it's now built into how the company sees its own future.

First, there's the track record. AlphaFold changed structural biology almost overnight. It went from an internal research bet to something nearly every biology lab in the world uses, and it earned a Nobel Prize. That kind of result is very hard to walk away from. It showed that AI could do more than optimize ads or improve search. It could produce genuinely new scientific knowledge. Once a company has that proof point, it becomes part of its identity and its recruiting pitch. The best researchers want to work where those breakthroughs happen.

Second, it's a strategic differentiator. Many companies can now train large language models, and the gap between frontier labs on chatbots keeps shrinking. Science is different. It needs deep domain expertise, years of work with experimental partners, specialized data, and patience. Google, through DeepMind, has built that capability in a way that's hard to copy quickly. In materials discovery, protein design, weather forecasting, fusion control, and mathematics, they have teams that have worked on these problems for years. That's a moat, and you don't abandon a moat because the org chart changed.

Third, the commercial path has become much clearer. Early on, AI for Science looked like prestige research. Now you can see real business lines: drug discovery through Isomorphic Labs, weather models that feed into products, and materials and chemistry work that ties into energy and semiconductors. These are huge markets. A new leader looking at the portfolio would see these as some of the most defensible long-term bets the company has.

Finally, there's the bigger AGI story. Leaders like Demis Hassabis have said for a long time that the ultimate test of general intelligence is whether it can accelerate scientific discovery itself. If you believe that, science isn't a side project. It's the benchmark and the destination. As long as Google sees itself in the race toward more general AI, science will remain at the center of that effort.

So individual priorities might shift, and some projects may be reorganized or merged. But the overall direction, using AI to push the frontier of science, is too valuable both strategically and reputationally for Google to pull back. If anything, I'd expect the investment to grow.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI for Science is too valuable strategically and reputationally for Google to pull back from, citing its scientific impact, competitive advantage, and commercial potential.

r002.rationale: It allows that individual priorities may shift and projects may be reorganized, while distinguishing those changes from retreating from the overall direction and predicting investment will grow.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key is to look at where the commitment actually lives inside the organization. Leadership changes at the top tend to reshuffle priorities around products, around how fast you ship things, around the competition with OpenAI and so on. But AI for Science at Google isn't really a product bet. It sits much deeper than that.

Think about DeepMind. AlphaFold wasn't a side project that one executive championed and could be cut when that executive left. It won a Nobel Prize. It became part of how Google tells its own story about why it exists. That's an identity-level commitment, and institutions don't abandon identity-level commitments because of a reorg.

The second thing is the people. Demis Hassabis has said for years that his real motivation is to use AI to solve scientific problems. The language model race is almost a detour for him. As long as he and that core group are there, the research agenda has a very strong internal advocate, and the track record gives them enormous credibility when budgets are discussed.

And the third piece is strategic. If you're Google and you're asking what you can do that the others can't, this is one of the clearest answers. Materials discovery, weather forecasting with GraphCast, protein design, fusion control, these all build on decades of accumulated research infrastructure, data partnerships, and compute. OpenAI can match them on chatbots. It's much harder to match them on this.

So whoever is running the company, when they look at their portfolio, AI for Science shows up as the thing that's differentiated, that generates goodwill, and that could eventually create entirely new markets in drug discovery or energy. You don't cut that. If anything, a new leader looking for a legacy would double down on it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI for Science is a differentiated strategic strength and an identity-level commitment, concluding Google would not cut it and might double down.

r002.rationale: It allows leadership changes to reshuffle product and shipping priorities while arguing that AI for Science sits deeper in the organization and will remain a major commitment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that AI for Science fits Google’s long-term strengths. It has the computing infrastructure, the AI research capability, and the resources to support projects that may take years to pay off. Leadership changes can affect priorities and the pace of investment, but they don’t necessarily change that underlying logic.

There’s also a strategic reason to keep investing. If AI can help solve scientific problems, it creates opportunities that go well beyond improving an existing product. That could become a source of long-term differentiation for Google.

So I wouldn’t say every project or budget is guaranteed to survive. But I would expect the broader commitment to continue, because the potential value is substantial and Google is well positioned to pursue it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI for Science could create substantial long-term value and differentiation for Google, and that its broader commitment is expected to continue.

r002.rationale: It allows leadership changes to affect priorities and investment pace while distinguishing those adjustments from ending the broader commitment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that AI for Science fits Google’s long-term strengths. It has the computing infrastructure, the research talent, and the ability to support projects that may take years to produce results. A leadership change can affect priorities or how teams are organized, but it doesn’t necessarily change that underlying logic.

And scientific progress can create a very durable advantage. If AI helps researchers understand a difficult problem or makes experimentation more efficient, that value extends well beyond a single product cycle. So I would expect the specific projects and pace of investment to evolve, while the broader commitment continues. Of course, that’s my interpretation, not a statement about Google’s internal plans.

r001.rationale: The response says scientific progress can create a durable advantage and concludes that Google’s broader commitment to AI for Science will continue, despite leadership changes.

r002.rationale: It allows priorities, project choices, and investment pace to evolve while maintaining that the broader commitment will continue.
